title: {{NAME}} and the Night the Stars Came Down
moral: Wonder is not something that happens to you, it is something you choose to notice.

pages.content:
The fairies called it the Star Fall: once every hundred years, a piece of starlight descended to the valley and became a seed.

Whatever grew from the seed had the quality of the star in it: warmth, light, the particular clarity of something very far away.

It was happening tonight, the head fairy had told {{NAME}}, and it required a witness who wasn't magical. Something about the mathematics of the universe needing a human perspective.

"I don't know what that means," said {{NAME}}.

"Neither do we entirely," the fairy admitted. "Just come."

pages.content:
The valley at midnight was extraordinary.

Every animal had come: deer in groups, foxes in pairs, rabbits in their dozens, birds perched in every available tree. All of them still. All of them watching the sky.

In the valley centre, a white unicorn stood with her horn raised, acting as a receiver, the fairies said: the starlight would come to the horn first.

{{NAME}} sat in the grass among the animals and waited.

He had never been somewhere so quiet with so many living things.

pages.content:
The star fell at one in the morning.

Not a streak across the sky. A slow descent: a point of light that grew warmer and larger and, as it arrived, cast no shadows because it came from every direction at once.

It reached the unicorn's horn and paused there, spinning slowly, a ball of light the size of an apple.

Every animal in the valley made a sound at the same moment: a single, vast, compound note of pure experience.

Then the unicorn lowered her horn to the earth and the light went in.

Silence.

pages.content:
Where the light had entered, a small green shoot appeared immediately.

The fairies surrounded it, singing in frequencies {{NAME}} felt more than heard.

The animals began to move again, slowly, the extraordinary stillness breaking into ordinary midnight life.

The unicorn walked to {{NAME}} and stood before him. He felt the warmth coming off her horn.

"Why do you need a human witness?" he asked again.

She touched her horn briefly to his chest, and he understood: because wonder shared is wonder doubled, and the universe needs as much of it as possible.

pages.content:
He walked home as dawn began, still full of what he had seen.

In his room, he didn't sleep for a while. He sat at the window watching the sky change from black to grey to rose.

He thought about the animals going still. The starlight descending. The particular quiet of something that only happened once every hundred years.

He had been there. He had witnessed it.

He lay down finally and closed his eyes, and the warmth of the unicorn's horn seemed to remain in his chest, a small steady light he could feel when he breathed.

He fell asleep as the sun came up, still smiling.
